guide_sections.heading: Business date versus UTC date
guide_sections.body:
Three orders taken by a New York store on one evening, stored as instants:

```text
local clock (New York)   stored instant (UTC)   business date   UTC date
2025-01-15 09:30 EST     2025-01-15 14:30       2025-01-15      2025-01-15
2025-01-15 21:00 EST     2025-01-16 02:00       2025-01-15      2025-01-16
2025-01-15 23:59 EST     2025-01-16 04:59       2025-01-15      2025-01-16
```

Grouping by `as.Date(x, tz = "UTC")` reports one order on January 15 and two on January 16, even though the store took all three before it closed on the 15th. `as.Date(x, tz = "America/New_York")` puts all three on the 15th, which is what the daily sales report should show. Passing tz explicitly also means the result does not depend on a default.

Chronology is unaffected by either choice. Sorting the stored instants gives 09:30, 21:00, 23:59 whichever zone is used for display, because a zone only changes how a count of seconds is printed. Keep the instant for ordering and joins, derive the business date with a stated zone, and write that zone next to the report so the next reader does not regroup the rows with a different one.

exercises.approach: Parse the first starter value with `as.Date()` and add 1. Date arithmetic counts whole calendar days, so no time of day or zone is involved.
exercises.why: 2024 is divisible by 4 and is not a century year, so February has 29 days. One day after 2024-02-28 is therefore 2024-02-29, and the starter's second value, 2024-03-01, is two days after the first rather than one.
exercises.wrong: Incrementing the day field of the string and rolling over to March after day 28. That produces 2024-03-01 and silently drops leap day, which is exactly the boundary this input was chosen to test.

exercises.approach: Parse the timestamp with an explicit format and `tz = "UTC"`, then add 7200, because arithmetic on POSIXct values is in seconds.
exercises.why: UTC never shifts for daylight saving, so two clock hours and two elapsed hours agree for this instant. 12:00 becomes 14:00 on the same date, and difftime reports the gap in the unit that was asked for rather than one R picks.
exercises.wrong: Writing `instant + 2` to mean two hours. POSIXct counts seconds, so the result is 12:00:02, a value that looks almost unchanged when printed to the minute and is easy to miss in review.
exercises.verify: `as.numeric(difftime(instant + 7200, instant, units = "hours"))` returns 2, and `format(instant + 7200, "%H:%M", tz = "UTC")` shows "14:00".

exercises.approach: Parse "2025-01-15" with `as.Date()` and keep it as a Date, since the source records a day and no time of day.
exercises.why: A Date carries no zone, so it prints as 2025-01-15 in every session and on every machine. Its arithmetic is in days, which is what a due date or a reporting day needs.
exercises.wrong: Storing the day as `as.POSIXct("2025-01-15", tz = "UTC")`. That invents a midnight UTC time, and formatting it for New York shows 2025-01-14 19:00, moving the record to the previous day.

exercises.approach: Ask the data owner for the source zone, then check whether each label falls in the skipped spring hour or the repeated autumn hour and apply a written policy: reject, or choose the earlier or later offset.
exercises.why: In New York the labels 02:00 to 02:59 never occurred on 2025-03-09, and 01:00 to 01:59 occurred twice on 2025-11-02, first as EDT and then as EST. A bare "2025-11-02 01:30" therefore names two instants one hour apart, and nothing in the text says which.
exercises.wrong: Parsing without tz. R then uses the session zone, so the same file yields different instants on a laptop set to UTC and on a server set to New York, and a nonexistent label may become NA or shift depending on the platform.
exercises.verify: `format(as.POSIXct(c("2025-11-02 05:30", "2025-11-02 06:30"), tz = "UTC"), "%H:%M %Z", tz = "America/New_York")` shows "01:30 EDT" and "01:30 EST", one label for two instants.

exercises.approach: Parse with an explicit format, then count results that are NA where the raw text was not, and stop or report those rows before any date arithmetic.
exercises.why: With a format supplied, `as.Date("not-a-date", format = "%Y-%m-%d")` returns NA and raises no error, so the program keeps running unless the result is inspected. The NA would later vanish from a grouped count or make a range NA.
exercises.wrong: Relying on as.Date to fail loudly. Without a format it stops only when the first non-missing value matches no default format; if an earlier row parses, later bad rows quietly become NA, and with a format no row ever errors.
exercises.verify: `is.na(as.Date("not-a-date", format = "%Y-%m-%d"))` returns TRUE, and `sum(is.na(parsed) & !is.na(raw))` shows how many rows failed.

exercises.approach: Keep the UTC instant as the canonical column for ordering, and derive a separate business date with `as.Date(instant, tz = "America/New_York")` for grouping and labels.
exercises.why: The reference instant, 12:00 UTC, is 07:00 in New York on the same date, but an order at 02:00 UTC on January 16 belongs to the store's January 15. Ordering uses the stored seconds, which no display zone changes, so both columns can coexist without conflict.
exercises.wrong: Sorting by the formatted local clock text. On 2025-11-02 an event at 01:45 EDT happened before one at 01:15 EST, yet the strings sort 01:15 first, reversing the true order.
exercises.verify: `as.Date(as.POSIXct("2025-01-16 02:00", tz = "UTC"), tz = "America/New_York")` returns 2025-01-15, and `as.numeric(instant + 1) > as.numeric(instant)` returns TRUE.
